    Important Words
    • vāsudeva - dhiyā — thinking of Lord Vāsudeva
      Compound: Vāsudeva + dhī (intellection, consideration). Nanda mentally substitutes Uddhava for Kṛṣṇa. Gauḍīyas read this as the textual model for guru-dhī, vaiṣṇava-dhī, prasāda-dhī — the trained capacity to see Kṛṣṇa through what carries Him.
    • pariṣvajya — embracing
      Gerund of pari-√svaj (to embrace fully, around). Not a polite namaskāra but a full-armed embrace — the bodily gesture of vātsalya. Nanda's body knows what to do before his mind interprets the visitor.
    • anucaram — the follower
      Accusative of anucara — one who walks after. Uddhava is the anucara of Kṛṣṇa; in Nanda's eyes that title confers Kṛṣṇa-quality. Gauḍīya etiquette: the anucara is honored with the honor due the master.
    • priyam — dear
      Accusative of priya. Priya here is transferred property — Uddhava is dear to Kṛṣṇa, therefore dear to Nanda. The whole social grammar of Vraja runs on this transitivity of priyatā.
    • prītaḥ — happy
      Past participle of √prī. The same root as priya. Nanda's prīti at seeing Uddhava is the surfacing of his prīti for the One who sent him — the messenger becomes the visible form of a hidden joy.
    • ārcayat — worshiped
      Imperfect of √arc. Not merely 'received' or 'entertained' — Nanda offers arcana, formal worship, to a man he could (as elder, as king of cowherds) have merely embraced. The grammar measures how completely vātsalya treats Kṛṣṇa's friend as Kṛṣṇa.
    As soon as Uddhava arrived at Nanda Mahārāja’s home, Nanda came forward to meet him. The cowherd King embraced him in great happiness and worshiped him as nondifferent from Lord Vāsudeva.
    Purport

    Uddhava looked just like Nanda’s son Kṛṣṇa and gave pleasure to anyone who saw him. Thus although Nanda was absorbed in thoughts of separation from Kṛṣṇa, when he saw Uddhava coming toward his house, he became aware of external events and eagerly went out to embrace his exalted visitor.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    As soon as Uddhava arrived at Nanda Mahārāja's home, Nanda came forward to meet him. The cowherd King embraced him in great happiness and worshiped him as nondifferent from Lord Vāsudeva.
    Commentary

    Then Uddhava entered the house of Nanda, which revealed the misery due to separation from Krsna. Nanda emerged from within the house, and saw that Uddhava appeared very much like his own son. Because of the energy given by the bliss of seeing him, he was able to execute the external behavior and conversations. Thinking of Uddhava as guest, who was worthy of worship like Narayana (vasudeva dhih), Nanda worshiped Uddhava with footwash and other items.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    When Uddhava arrived at the door, Nanda heard from inside the house and came there. Uddhava was Kṛṣṇa’s devotee (anucaram) and dear to him, being like Kṛṣṇa’s own self. Or he was dear to Nanda since he was non-different from Kṛṣṇa, being the abode of Kṛṣṇa as a devotee.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    When Uddhava arrived at the door, Nanda rose and met him. Since his chariot came unnoticed, he simply arrived without Nanda knowing beforehand. He was a dear devotee of Kṛṣṇa, or dear to Nanda. It is the nature of devotees to worship guests. Thus he treated him as the Lord. Or he thought that Kṛṣṇa had arrived.

    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    When a long-absent son's closest friend appears at the door, the father runs out before any servant can announce him. Nanda does not greet Uddhava as a guest — he embraces him as Vāsudeva Himself. In vātsalya-rasa, every messenger from the son carries the son's substance.

    Stories
    Bharata embracing the wooden sandals

    When Rāma left for the forest, Bharata installed His sandals on the throne and ruled in His name, embracing them as the king Himself (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyā-kāṇḍa). The relic of the beloved was treated as the beloved.

    Nanda's vāsudeva-dhiyā embrace of Uddhava is the vātsalya-side counterpart: anything that has touched Kṛṣṇa is Kṛṣṇa for the heart that loves Him. Gauḍīya prasāda-ethic stands on this same principle.

    Important Words
    • parama - annena — with first-class food
      Compound: parama (supreme) + anna (food). For a cowherd village, parama-anna means the best of milk, butter, curd, rice — Vraja's particular bhojana. The chapter's later focus on the morning's churning (44-46) is anticipated by this evening's parama-anna.
    • kaśipau — on a nice bed
      Locative of kaśipu — a soft cushion or couch. Same word that names the demon Hiraṇyakaśipu (he-who-likes-soft-beds). Here it returns to its innocent meaning: Vraja's hospitality, not Daitya luxury.
    • śramam — fatigue
      Accusative of śrama. The verse names the very state Nanda removes before asking his question — Uddhava's body is restored before his words are asked of him. Bhakti-etiquette: never extract speech from a tired guest.
    • pāda - saṁvāhana — foot-massage
      Compound: pāda (foot) + saṁvāhana (rubbing). In classical India this service is performed by a junior to a senior — Nanda the elder king performing it on Uddhava the younger guest is a deliberate inversion. The vātsalya-frame supersedes age and rank.
    • paryapṛcchat — he inquired
      Imperfect of pari-√prach. The prefix pari- intensifies: not a casual question but a full surrounding inquiry. The next twelve verses are the unfolding of this single paryapṛcchat — Nanda's heart opening verse by verse.
    • sukham — comfortably
      Adverbial accusative of sukha. Uddhava is comfortable when the questions begin. The very vocabulary will be contradicted by the end of the conversation, when Nanda himself becomes prema-prasara-vihvalaḥ (27) — comfort yields to overwhelm.
    After Uddhava had eaten first-class food, been seated comfortably on a bed and been relieved of his fatigue by a foot massage and other means, Nanda inquired from him as follows.
    Purport

    Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī mentions that Nanda had a servant massage Uddhava’s feet, since Uddhava was Nanda’s nephew.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After Uddhava had eaten first-class food, been seated comfortably on a bed and been relieved of his fatigue by a foot massage and other means, Nanda inquired from him as follows.
    Commentary

    Nanda fed Uddhava rice cooked in milk. From the day that Krsna had departed from Mathura, the kitchens of the people of Vraja were left unswept and dirty, filled with leaves, grass, dust and spider webs. The people of Vraja maintained their lives by buttermilk, yogurt and milk given by neighbors. They simply lamented, "We have died." But on this particular day, understanding Nanda’s anxiety that when Uddhava comes he should not suffer from hunger, one brahmana accompanying Nanda cooked a quantity of broken rice with milk for one person. Massaging Uddhava’s feet was performed by a servant, since Uddhava was his nephew and therefore an inferior.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He fed him rice boiled in milk or the best rice. Nanda offered him a bed and, when he spread out his body, he made him relax. He removed his fatigue by massaging his feet. When he was seated comfortably (sukham) he inquired from him.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He fed Uddhava rice because it was the principal food, as well as dairy products and other foods. He was seated on a bed or stretched his body out on the bed. He had others massage his feet or personally did it, and fanned him and offered sandalwood. When Uddhava’s fatigue was gone, Nanda inquired with lamentation.

    Important Words
    • śūra - nandanaḥ — the son of Śūra
      Compound: Śūra (Vasudeva's father) + nandana (son/delight). Nanda names Vasudeva by his patronymic — a respectful distance, the courtesy of a cowherd toward Yadu nobility. The verse preserves the social register Nanda inhabits.
    • muktaḥ — freed
      Past participle of √muc. Vasudeva was imprisoned by Kaṁsa for years; Nanda is asking after his release. Gauḍīyas note that the word mukta in 10.46 is bodily liberation from a tyrant — not the Advaitin mukti, which the chapter's later tattva-section will quietly reframe.
    • apatya - ādyaiḥ — with his children and so on
      Compound: apatya (offspring) + ādi (and so on). Nanda asks whether Vasudeva is rejoined with his sons — meaning Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, the boys Nanda himself raised. The phrasing is generous and painful at once: he calls them Vasudeva's offspring, not his own.
    • kuśalī — well
      Nominative of kuśalin — one possessing kuśala (well-being). The standard formal opening of any inquiry. But behind the formality is a father testing whether the word 'well' is now usable in his own household at all.
    • suhṛt - vrataḥ — devoted to his friends
      Compound: suhṛt (well-wisher) + vrata (vow). Nanda credentials Vasudeva by his fidelity to friendship — the very virtue Nanda himself is now living out by receiving Vasudeva's son's messenger with such honor.
    • mahā - bhāga — O most fortunate one
      Vocative compound: mahā (great) + bhāga (share, fortune). Nanda addresses Uddhava as 'most fortunate' — and the chapter will quietly establish that the fortune in question is that of being near Kṛṣṇa, which Nanda himself once had and now does not.
    [Nanda Mahārāja said:] My dear most fortunate one, does the son of Śūra fare well, now that he is free and has rejoined his children and other relatives?
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Nanda Mahārāja said:] My dear most fortunate one, does the son of Śūra fare well, now that he is free and has rejoined his children and other relatives?
    Commentary

    Fearing that if he asked about Krsna, his throat would choke up and tears would come to his eyes, Nanda first asked about the welfare of Vasudeva. Vasudeva was now freed from the prison house of Kamsa, and from all sorts of dangers.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Being unable to ask directly and immediately about Kṛṣṇa because of increased grief of separation, Nanda first asks about the welfare of Vasudeva as an introduction. O greatly fortunate Uddhava! You are qualified with great fortune since you are close to Kṛṣṇa. We however are not qualified for such fortune. Thus we are suitable to be rejected by him. As the son of Śūra Vasudeva has manifested his father’s good fortune, since Kṛṣṇa acts as his son. He is free from all dangers and united with his children (Kṛṣṇa). He is surrounded by friends (including Kṛṣṇa). Is he well? In this way he asks generally about everyone and also the condition of Kṛṣṇa.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Nanda asked about Vasudeva first since he was Kṛṣṇa’s father and Nanda’s friend. Or if he asked about Kṛṣṇa first he would be overcome with pain and would not be able to ask about other things after that. Or he asked the easy questions first since the question about Kṛṣṇa would be extensive. Or he had many worries about his dear friend Vasudeva because of his affection and thus asked about him first. O fortunate one! You are greatly fortunate because you are dear to Kṛṣṇa. We however are unfortunate since he gave us up. He does not mention Vasudeva’s name directly because of his friendship and respect or because of natural affection. He also asks about children and wives (ādyaiḥ). Vasudeva has been freed from all dangers and joined with children and relatives. He is surrounded by the Yadus. He asks about the welfare of Kṛṣṇa by asking about the welfare of all the Yadus and family members like Devakī.

    Important Words
    • diṣṭyā — by good fortune
      Instrumental of diṣṭi (destiny, ordained). A Sanskrit interjection of gratitude for providential outcome — 'thank heavens.' Nanda credits not Kṛṣṇa's strength but daiva, the divine arrangement; the cowherd refuses to praise the son to the son's friend.
    • pāpaḥ — the sinful (Kaṁsa)
      Nominative of pāpa. Kaṁsa is named by his moral substance, not his throne. Gauḍīya tīkā: Nanda's denunciation is mild — pāpaḥ, not asura or daitya — because vātsalya-rasa preserves the cowherd's structural innocence; he does not enter the language of demonology.
    • svena-pāpmanā — by his own sinfulness
      Compound: sva (own) + pāpman (sinfulness, instrumental). Theological correctness: Kaṁsa is killed not by Kṛṣṇa's anger but by his own karma working through Kṛṣṇa. The doctrine of svakṛta-doṣa stated in passing.
    • sādhūnām — of the saintly
      Genitive plural of sādhu. Nanda calls the Yadus sādhus — a courtly compliment, but also a quiet self-distancing. He does not call himself a sādhu; vātsalya speaks from a more domestic register.
    • dharma - śīlānām — of those always righteous in behavior
      Compound: dharma + śīla (character). The Yadus are credentialed by śīla, not by power. Gauḍīyas note that Vraja's vocabulary praises others' character abundantly and its own not at all — humility is structural to the rasa.
    • dveṣṭi — hated
      Third-person singular of √dviṣ. The verb of hatred — used of Kaṁsa, never reciprocated by the Yadus or Kṛṣṇa. The Bhāgavatam preserves a strict asymmetry: dveṣa is the demonic emotion; the divine response to it is līlā-vadha, not counter-dveṣa.
    Fortunately, because of his own sins, the sinful Kaṁsa has been killed, along with all his brothers. He always hated the saintly and righteous Yadus.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Fortunately, because of his own sins, the sinful Kaṁsa has been killed, along with all his brothers. He always hated the saintly and righteous Yadus.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    In order to maintain self control, Nanda praises the main cause of Vasudeva being freed, putting the direct topic of Kṛṣṇa at a distance temporarily. Since Kaṁsa died because he was sinful, there was no fault in killing him. His sin was hatred of those of proper conduct (innocent people) and those following dharma. Therefore we permitted Kṛṣṇa to go to Mathurā.

    Important Words
    • smarati — remembers
      Third-person singular present of √smṛ. The verse repeats smaraṇa-vocabulary that has now spread through the chapter (4, 5, 21, 27). Vraja's question is always the smaraṇa-question: do we still exist inside the Lord's smṛti?
    • mātaram — His mother
      Accusative of mātṛ. Nanda lists mother before himself — the father will not yet name himself in the litany. Even in grief, vātsalya defers to vātsalya: Yaśodā's claim on Kṛṣṇa is named first.
    • vrajam — Vraja
      The dhāma itself enters the list of remembered objects. Gauḍīyas read this verse as Nanda placing the dhāma alongside persons — the place is loved, and asked-after, on the same footing as the people. Vraja is not scenery.
    • ātma - nātham — whose master is Himself
      Compound modifying vrajam: Vraja whose only nātha (lord/protector) is Kṛṣṇa Himself. Theological force: even in His absence, Vraja has no other lord. Gauḍīya tradition makes this verse a proof-text for kṛṣṇa-nātha exclusivity in Vraja.
    • gāvaḥ — the cows
      Nominative plural of go. The cows enter the list before Govardhana — Nanda's instinct is correct: the gāvaḥ are the persons of Vraja, not its property. Gauḍīya cow-theology stands on such moments.
    • girim — the mountain (Govardhana)
      Accusative of giri. Govardhana, the hill Kṛṣṇa lifted seven days; the verse names it last, almost as climax. The hill that knew Kṛṣṇa's hand most intimately — does it now know His memory?
    Does Kṛṣṇa remember us? Does He remember His mother and His friends and well-wishers? Does He remember the cowherds and their village of Vraja, of which He is the master? Does He remember the cows, Vṛndāvana forest and Govardhana Hill?
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Does Kṛṣṇa remember us? Does He remember His mother and His friends and well-wishers? Does He remember the cowherds and their village of Vraja, of which He is the master? Does He remember the cows, Vṛndāvana forest and Govardhana Hill?
    Commentary

    Then with tears in his eyes and choked voice he began to ask about Krsna. Pointing with his finger, he said, "Just see the condition of Krsna’s mother. See Vraja now, bereft of glory, whose master was Krsna (atma natham), but which is now without Krsna." !9. "Will Krsna come here? O Uddhava, do you know the intention in Krsna’s mind?" "Yes I know, he will come. He will relieve you of suffering and will stay here." "Let him not console us, and let him not stay here permanently. I beg only to see him. We, his own people (sva janana), afflicted by separation, will die today or tomorrow. Will he not come to see them just once? Oh Govinda, please take (vindatam) unlimited cows, meaning also millions of gold coins, pearls, and diamonds, jewel encrusted plates, various types of cloth, ornaments, sandalwood, aguru, kumkum and many household items. These are all yours. We are almost dead. Who else has a right to these things? Take all these things and live wherever you desire to live." "Why are you talking like this? You should know that he is about to come." Not being able to bear the delay, Nanda said, " When (karhi) will I be able to see his face? His face, which surpasses a million moons, his incomparable nose, his sweet smile, and his long, lotus petal eyes. As the end approaches, seeing this, we will die." By this he expresses his extreme anxiety.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Not able to control himself for long, Nanda then asked directly what he wanted to ask. Does Kṛṣṇa, who attracts all hearts, who is my son, remember us? Did he not forget us? Plural is used (naḥ) to indicate Upananda and others also. It thus indicates Kṛṣṇa’s affection for all. He mentions Yaśodā, since Nanda remembered her because of his pain on seeing her great sorrow. Does he remember other cowherd relatives like maternal uncles, his companions like Śrīdāmā, the cowherds in general and also the gopīs, and Vraja, whose master is Kṛṣṇa (ātma). By being master of Vraja he was naturally the master of everyone. Gāvaḥ should be gāḥ. He lists everyone from most important (Yaśodā) to less important (cows). Since it is included in Vṛndāvana, he mentions Govardhana after Vṛndāvana, though Govardhana is more important. Or he mentions naḥ first because that came to his mind first. Then he remembered about the Yaśodā, well-wishers and Kṛṣṇa’s friends in that order because of proximity to himself, with the later persons further away in open areas. Then, unable to remember details, he asks about other cowherds and Vraja in general. After asking in general about Vraja, not able to think of the details, he then asks specifically about the cows. Does he constantly remember Vṛndāvana where he enjoyed and the cows with whom he enjoyed, though he has now given them up? In Vṛndāvana, does he remember the mountain he held up in his hand for seven days, while encouraging worship of himself--a desire tree with a wealth of happiness and a variety of pastimes? After killing Kaṁsa, who was only one person, he is now hampered in many ways. He must not be able to think about himself because of worrying about a safe place for the Yadus, bringing them here and there, in order to defend them from many wicked enemies, such as followers of Kaṁsa’s wives and the father of Kaṁsa’s wives. In that condition how could he think of us?

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    A father's most painful question wears the disguise of a list: does he remember His mother, His friends, the cows, the hill, the forest? Each item is a hand reaching toward a son who has not come back. Nanda cannot ask 'does He love me?' so he asks 'does He remember the cows?'

    Stories
    Daśaratha's grief for Rāma

    When Rāma went to the forest, Daśaratha could not stop reciting the names of his son's companions, his bow, his sandals, his deer-skin (Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyā-kāṇḍa). The list-of-things became the only available form of the unutterable question.

    Nanda in SB 10.46.18 does the same. Gauḍīya ācāryas note that vātsalya-viraha and dāsa-vātsalya-viraha share this grammar of inventory: when the beloved is unspeakable, the heart names everything around him.

    Important Words
    • āyāsyati — will He come
      Third-person singular future of ā-√yā. The whole verse turns on this verb. Nanda's question is the entire eschatology of the chapter compressed: will He come back? The answer will be deferred till Uddhava's reply in verse 34.
    • govindaḥ — Govinda
      From go (cow) + √vid (to find, please). The cowherd-name of Kṛṣṇa. Nanda uses Govinda — not Kṛṣṇa, not Vāsudeva — because vātsalya speaks in the dhāma's native vocabulary. The Mathurā-Kṛṣṇa is not yet at home on Nanda's tongue.
    • sakṛt — once
      Adverb: 'a single time.' The smallness of the request measures the depth of the longing. Vipralambha asks for a single glance — not residence, not return. Gauḍīya tradition recognizes this sakṛt-asking as the signature of pure prema.
    • drakṣyāma — we may glance upon
      First-person plural future of √dṛś. The optative force: we might see. Nanda uses 'we,' folding Yaśodā and the whole village into his own prayer. Vraja never grieves singly.
    • su - nasam — with a beautiful nose
      Compound modifying vaktram. The Bhāgavatam itemizes the face — nose, smile, eyes — because in viraha the totality is unbearable; love survives by fragments. Gauḍīya alaṅkāra-śāstra recognizes this as aṅga-varṇana, limb-praise, the bhāva-stricken lover's prayer-form.
    • su - smita - īkṣaṇam — with a beautiful smile and (beautiful) eyes
      Compound: su (beautiful) + smita (smile) + īkṣaṇa (glance). Note that for Nanda the eyes are inseparable from the smile — Kṛṣṇa's gaze and Kṛṣṇa's amusement are remembered as one feature. The grammar refuses to split them.
    Will Govinda return even once to see His family? If He ever does, we may then glance upon His beautiful face, with its beautiful eyes, nose and smile.
    Purport

    Now that Kṛṣṇa had become a prince in the great city of Mathurā, Nanda had lost hope that He would come back to live in the simple cowherd village of Vṛndāvana. But he hoped against hope that Kṛṣṇa would come back at least once to visit the simple cowherd folk who had raised Him from birth.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Will Govinda return even once to see His family? If He ever does, we may then glance upon His beautiful face, with its beautiful eyes, nose and smile.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Nanda began to worry, “My son is grateful and intelligent. But also he said he had to satisfy his relatives in Mathurā (SB 10.45.23). This will cause some delay.” He then asked about some other pleasant result. Will Govinda return to see his people? Govinda is the protector of Gokula. He must return. He must return to see those who are objects of affection, his own people (sva-janān). Let him not come repeatedly. Will he come even once just to console everyone? Desire that he come to see them indicates that they are suffering as if from a serious illness. He should come at least once, since some inhabitants of Vraja may not continue to live. There are some among us who are in the process of dying, having given up hope of living, who suffer from not seeing him again. Others, who will live a little longer, suffer from the impossibility of again seeing him. In both cases, intolerable suffering from longing will be destroyed if he comes once. With his coming there will be another pleasant result. Nanda reveals this with agitation. If he will come at some time, then we will see his face. Instead of tarhi sometimes karhi is seen. Kṛṣṇa promised to come and see them (SB 10.45.23). Thus they would not go to Mathurā and see him. Remembering his face he remembers its beauty, almost fainting.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Thinking that Kṛṣṇa, being intelligent and grateful, will remember them at all times, he asks another urgent question. He is the king of Gokula (govindaḥ). Thus he must return. He must see the people who are objects of his affection (sva-janān). He must see them at least once, since they are suffering. Will he satisfy them with his sweet words? Or will he come to see us once, not doing anything else? We expect to see him once, and not anywhere else. This is a statement made in misery. “He sees everything. Even staying there he sees you at all times. Why should he come here?” We will see his beautiful eyes, smile and nose. Though all his limbs are beautiful, the nose and eyes being the chief limbs are mentioned to represent all his limbs. By his coming, our desires will be fulfilled completely. Out of great longing, and loss of control Nanda utters “When will this be (karhi—instead of tarhi)?” Asking this question, they expect to see him in Vraja.

    A father imagines his son's face the way a parched traveler imagines water — nose, smile, eyes — feature by feature, because the whole is too much to hold at once. The promise Nanda asks for is small: 'come once, that we may glance.' Vipralambha asks for almost nothing — and asks for it endlessly.

    Important Words
    • dāva - agneḥ — from the forest fire
      Compound: dāva (forest) + agni (fire). The forest fire that Kṛṣṇa swallowed (SB 10.17, 10.19). Nanda lists the events chronologically; the chapter assumes the reader knows the canto and reads each item as cross-reference.
    • vāta - varṣāt — from the wind and rain
      Compound: vāta (wind) + varṣa (rain). The Indra-storm at Govardhana (SB 10.25). Nanda's verse mentions the danger but not yet Indra by name; the offended deity is too elevated to invoke in a cowherd's complaint.
    • vṛṣa — from the bull (Ariṣṭa)
      Bull-demon Ariṣṭa, killed in SB 10.36. The verse uses the bare vṛṣa — the demon-bull, not Kṛṣṇa's own divine bull-form — and trusts the reader to disambiguate by context.
    • sarpāt — from the serpent (Kāliya / Aghāsura)
      Ablative of sarpa. Could indicate Kāliya (SB 10.16) or Aghāsura (SB 10.12). Gauḍīya commentators read the singular as deliberately ambiguous — Vraja's serpents were many; Kṛṣṇa met them all.
    • su - mahā - ātmanā — by the very great soul
      Compound: su (very) + mahā (great) + ātman. A Bhāgavata-honorific that bridges aiśvarya and mādhurya. Nanda uses it of his own son — the verse stages how vātsalya can voice the Lord's mahima without losing intimacy.
    • rakṣitāḥ — protected
      Past participle of √rakṣ. The verb of refuge — same root as rakṣaka, kṛṣṇa-rakṣaka. Nanda's identity is constituted by being among the rakṣitāḥ; gopāla-protection is not metaphor in Vraja but lived autobiography.
    We were saved from the forest fire, the wind and rain, the bull and serpent demons — from all such insurmountable, deadly dangers — by that very great soul, Kṛṣṇa.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    We were saved from the forest fire, the wind and rain, the bull and serpent demons—from all such insurmountable, deadly dangers—by that very great soul, Kṛṣṇa.
    Commentary

    "But you will not die. You will live a long time, raising your son with affection." "Now, we will not be saved from the hands of death." In saying this he recounts the previous threats of death. "He saves us from the forest fire, from the rains produced by Indra, because of his natural affection for us (su mahatmaha). But today, why does he not save us from the huge fire of terrible separation? I cannot understand this."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    As if gaining self control. Nanda remembering Kṛṣṇa’s great affection for his relatives which made him forget his own suffering, in order to console himself. But then, by that remembrance he laments as if his heart as been broken. From his young childhood Kṛṣṇa performed many acts to save us. I will describe some. From the beginning he showed great compassion. He protected us from the forest fire, because of his powers similar to Nārāyaṇa’s as stated by Garga. Or, seeing the fire, he swallowed the fire which became nectar for him, because of his very nature or his compassion. Similarly he protected us from the wind and rain, from the bull and snake, and from other personifications of death. He was the most excellent, great soul, having natural qualities such as unconditional love, mercy and power.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Having described Kṛṣṇa’s form with desire to see him, he describes his qualities, somewhat lamenting. He describes these events since he personally experienced them. The snake refers to Kāliya and Aghāsura. These were equal to death. We are alive because he saved us. He could save us because his nature is mercy (su-mahātmanā). We were saved because he is compassionate, not because of our qualities. This is a statement uttered in misery.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    A father lists the times his son saved the family: forest fire, storm, the bull-demon, the serpent. He is not boasting — he is testifying. Vraja's claim on Kṛṣṇa is not theological; it is the record of every danger from which He pulled them out. Love built on rescue.

    Stories
    Gajendra rescued

    When the king of elephants was seized by the crocodile, he cried 'I do not pray as anyone's owner or relative — I pray as the helpless' (SB 8.3). Viṣṇu descended on Garuḍa and cut the jaws.

    Nanda's verse-20 list is the Vraja-version of Gajendra's testimony: 'He saved us, we are the saved.' Gauḍīya theology of śaraṇāgati grounds itself in such enumerations — the surrendered are those who can name what they were rescued from.

    Important Words
    • kṛṣṇa - vīryāṇi — the valorous deeds of Kṛṣṇa
      Compound: Kṛṣṇa + vīrya (heroic deeds). The technical term for the līlā-katha that bhakti-tradition recommends as the object of śravaṇa-smaraṇa. SB 1.5.22 anchors: idaṁ hi puṁsas tapasaḥ śrutasya … yad uttamaśloka-guṇānuvarṇanam.
    • līlā - apāṅga - nirīkṣitam — (His) playful sidelong glance
      Compound: līlā (play) + apāṅga (corner-of-the-eye) + nirīkṣita (looking). The single most-prized rasa-feature of Kṛṣṇa in Gauḍīya kāvya: not the front-gaze but the slanted, half-amused glance. The whole tradition of Rādhā's catching that glance derives from such verses.
    • hasitam — smiling
      Past participle of √has. Kṛṣṇa's mandasmita is itself a defined rasa-feature. Nanda lists it third in his stack of remembered things — the smile, like the glance, can be remembered separately from the face.
    • bhāṣitam — speaking
      Past participle of √bhāṣ. The words themselves are remembered — not their content but their fact. Vraja's hearts treat kṛṣṇa-vacana as a remembered object, not merely a transmitted information.
    • śithilāḥ — slackened
      Adjective: loosened, gone slack. Same word used for ropes that no longer bind. The hands of Vraja slacken on their tasks; smaraṇa is the un-tightening of worldly grip. Gauḍīya tīkā: this is the verse where the chapter teaches bhakti's strange anti-physics — the more love, the less effort can be exerted on anything else.
    • kriyāḥ — material activities
      Nominative plural of kriyā. Same word that names the ritual actions of varṇāśrama. The verse does not say bhakti destroys kriyās; it says smaraṇa makes them go slack. A subtler doctrine — and the one the gopīs in verse 4 already perfected.
    As we remember the wonderful deeds Kṛṣṇa performed, His playful sidelong glances, His smiles and His words, O Uddhava, we forget all our material engagements.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    As we remember the wonderful deeds Kṛṣṇa performed, His playful sidelong glances, His smiles and His words, O Uddhava, we forget all our material engagements.
    Commentary

    "By the nectar of remembrance of his moonlike face, all pain will vanish." "That is true, but though remembering him removes all suffering, now that remembrance gives us more suffering, by great misfortune. When we remember him, we lose all interest in everything. Though we continue to bathe, eat and perform other daily activities by rote, we have lost interest in these things also. In this state we cannot remain alive."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    In two verses Nanda remembers his powers and his sweetness. Remembering both, he becomes agitated. He informs Uddhava of his daily suffering. We remember Kṛṣṇa’s prowess. The word “Kṛṣṇa” should also be supplied to the other items. Nanda was unable to say Kṛṣṇa’s name repeatedly. He showed prowess in swallowing the fire. Not only did he show heroic acts, but also sweetness such as playful glances in one direction out of shyness. He attentively glanced everywhere with affection. At the same time he smiled. And then he spoke. Remembering that, and then experiencing pain, we stop our work. Because of inner disturbance, external actions stop. This has been arranged by the Lord. We should remain healthy by engagement and thinking of other things, but we cannot do that.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After describing his pastimes, Nanda shows Kṛṣṇa’s attractiveness, and his own misery. We remember his astonishing deeds such as killing Pūtanā. The word Kṛṣṇa applies to all the elements listed (his glances, smiles and words) though it is in one compound only. Līlā means very playful. All of these elements were very attractive to the heart. The order is with increasing excellent (words being most attractive). This is clear from statements like the following. madhurayā girā valgu-vākyayā budha-manojṣayā puṣkarekṣaṇa vidhi-karīr imā vīra muhyatīr adhara-sīdhunāpyāyayasva naḥ O lotus-eyed one, by your sweet voice and charming words, which attract the minds of the intelligent, we have fainted. Our dear hero, please revive your maidservants with the nectar of your lips. SB 10.31.8 In speaking, the smiles and glances are also present. Actions can also refer to daily or periodic acts such as eating. By this remembrance we become slow in excuting duties. Or being distracted we cannot complete our actions.

    Important Words
    • mukunda — Mukunda
      From mukti + √dā (giver-of-liberation), but in Vraja vocabulary the etymology gives way to affection — Mukunda is the cowherd-name with sweet sound, like Govinda. Gauḍīyas note: Vraja uses moksa-vocabulary as endearment, draining it of its Vedāntic charge.
    • pada - bhūṣitān — ornamented by (His) feet
      Compound: pada (foot) + bhūṣita (ornamented). Theological inversion: ordinarily places ornament those who walk in them; here His feet ornament the places. Pāda-rajas-doctrine in compressed form.
    • ākrīḍān — the locations of (His) play
      Accusative plural of ākrīḍa — playground. Gauḍīya geography of Vraja is an ākrīḍa-map: every site is a coordinate of a specific līlā. The Bhāgavatam itself authorizes the later Gosvāmī work of recovering each location.
    • tat - ātmatām — total absorption in Him
      Compound: tat (Him) + ātmatā (the state of being-the-self-of). A precise term for samādhi-grade absorption. The verse claims that seeing Vraja's geography produces what yogīs labor for — Gauḍīya pramāṇa for the supremacy of dhāma-darśana over abstract dhyāna.
    • sarit — rivers
      The Yamunā primarily, but the plural includes Mānasī-gaṅgā and the smaller streams. Vraja-geography never names the rivers; it names the act of Kṛṣṇa in each. Theological grammar: water is identified by who waded in it.
    • vana — forests
      The twelve vanas of Vraja (Bhāṇḍīravana, Tālavana, etc.) are catalogued in Bhāgavata cross-references. The verse implies them without listing — Gauḍīya tradition fills in: each vana is the site of a specific named līlā.
    When we see the places where Mukunda enjoyed His sporting pastimes — the rivers, hills and forests He decorated with His feet — our minds become totally absorbed in Him.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When we see the places where Mukunda enjoyed His sporting pastimes—the rivers, hills and forests He decorated with His feet—our minds become totally absorbed in Him.
    Commentary

    "If this is the case, then I can understand that you are staying in the house and remembering Krsna too much. Therefore to give up dwelling on him so much, you should herd the cows and walk on the bank of the Yamuna." Fearing such a remark, Nanda said, "On seeing the river, the forest and other places (uddesah) where Krsna performed pastimes, our conscious becomes more absorbed in Krsna. We think more of Krsna (tad atmatam), and the pain of separation increases."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “You should give up just staying at home and remembering Kṛṣṇa. Instead, herd the cows and wander on the bank of the Yamunā.” Nanda answers with this verse. Doing such actions will offer no solution to our problems. We see places in the forests, mountains and river banks decorated with the foot prints of Kṛṣṇa who freed me from the python and Varuṇa (mukunda), since even today those prints are preserved by the lap of the earth deity out of affection. And we see the signs of his playing. All living entities see them, what to speak of us. When we see them we become absorbed in him, actually seeing his sphūrti. What are we to do?

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “You should give up remembering his activities.” When we see rivers like Yamunā, hills like Govardhana or forested areas like Kāmyavana, ornamented with the footmarks of he who gives the highest bliss (mukunda), my son, because he played there, our minds cannot give up thinking of him. Another version has govinda. As king of Gokula, he is the object of devotion of all people of Vraja. The footprints remained for a long time without disappearing. sva-mūrtyā loka-lāvaṇya- nirmuktyā locanaṁ nṛṇām gīrbhis tāḥ smaratāṁ cittaṁ padais tān īkṣatāṁ kriyāḥ I have stolen people’s eyes with my form which makes them reject all other beauty, stolen their voices and ears by my words, stolen their minds and stolen their movements of their bodies by the markings on my footprints. SB 11.1.6 Or seeing the various places of pastimes (ākrīḍān) decorated with his footprints, with a display of various types of beauty, our minds become filled with Mukunda.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    The rivers, hills, and forests of Vraja are not landscape but archive — every place a print of Kṛṣṇa's foot. To walk Vraja is to walk on Him. The mind, seeing the print, attains tat-ātmatā — identity-with-the-imprinter through the imprint.

    Stories
    Caitanya at the Yamunā and Govardhana

    When Mahāprabhu finally entered Vraja, He could not walk — He rolled in the dust, mistook every tree for Kṛṣṇa's tamāla, and asked the cowherds to point out each kuñja by name (CC Madhya 17-18). The very ground was Kṛṣṇa for Him.

    Gauḍīyas read SB 10.46.22 as the tattva of Mahāprabhu's dhāma-darśana: ākrīḍān-īkṣyamāṇānāṁ manaḥ yāti tat-ātmatām. Mind sees a place He played, mind attains absorption in Him. The dhāma is a sādhana.

    Important Words
    • manye — I think
      First-person singular present of √man. The verb of opinion, of provisional naming. Nanda offers his theory tentatively; vātsalya cannot dogmatize about its own son. Gauḍīya tīkā: manye is the polite under-statement that protects the bhāva.
    • sura - uttamau — two of the most elevated demigods
      Compound: sura (god) + uttama (highest). Nanda's best guess — devas of the highest grade. The Bhāgavatam quietly records the gap between his guess and the truth: Kṛṣṇa is not a deva at all but the source of all devas. The chapter's tattva-section will gently restate this.
    • gargasya-vacanam — the statement of Garga (Ṛṣi)
      Genitive of Garga + accusative of vacana. Cross-reference to SB 10.8.13 — Garga's nāmakaraṇa-prediction. The Bhāgavatam cites itself; Nanda's memory of Garga's words is the textual mechanism that keeps Kṛṣṇa partially veiled in Vraja.
    • mahat - arthāya — for a great purpose
      Compound: mahat (great) + artha (purpose). Nanda assigns a devic purpose — relieving the earth's burden, etc. He is correct in substance but small in scale: the artha is greater than he can name. Vātsalya understates.
    • prāptau — obtained, arrived
      Past participle dual, nominative — used of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma jointly. The verb implies a destined coming, not an ordinary birth. Even Nanda's downscaled guess preserves the avatāra-grammar of arrival.
    • iha — on this planet
      Adverb 'here.' Vraja-vātsalya names earth as 'here' and devaloka as 'there' — the cowherd inversion of cosmic hierarchy. The devas Nanda imagines have come to Vraja; the higher realm is the one he is standing in.
    In my opinion, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma must be two exalted demigods who have come to this planet to fulfill some great mission of the demigods. Such was foretold by Garga Ṛṣi.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    In my opinion, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma must be two exalted demigods who have come to this planet to fulfill some great mission of the demigods. Such was foretold by Garga Ṛṣi.
    Commentary

    By the sudden recollection of Krsna as the Lord, in contrast to his natural production of affection in separation, Nanda speaks with a sense of discrimination. "These two sons have appeared in my house (iha) by the good fortune of myself and Vasudeva, for the welfare of the devatas (suranam arthaya), such as killing Kamsa and other demons. This is according to the profound words of Garga."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Nanda again recollects Kṛṣṇa’s powers, hoping to cover his sweetness, since he fears that if he suddenly manifests his sweet form and strengthens his heart, it will be a cause of suffering because of the affection arising from thinking of him as a son. Or he speaks of his powers with a desire to glory him as a natural result of special affection arising from separation. That is described in four verses. I think that the two boys are some great persons equal to Nārāyaṇa, who have made an appearance of being born in my house (iha). This statement is an expression of Nanda’s natural and internal affection for Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma as his sons.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Overcome with pain, he considers that the cause of his pain is his affection, thinking of Kṛṣṇa as his son. In order to pacify his heart, he covers that conception of Kṛṣṇa as his son. Or he speaks in misery, thinking that he should be ignored because of his low position and Kṛṣṇa’s high position. The two words ca indicate equal importance of Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma. Both of them are most merciful and affectionate to their friends. But we are not worthy of being recognized. Having come to the material world (iha prāptau) they are Hari and Hara, Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa, or the two outstanding members of the caturvyūha for benefiting the devatās by relieving the burden of the earth. Should they not give benefit to us mortals as well? Or among devatās they are the best devatās (sūrānām surottamau). They have appeared in this world to benefit the devotees (mahad-arthāya)—the Yadus, not us devotees. This is a statement of extreme misery. Or he made us happy by his pastimes but, by giving us up, has produced the opposite result. He must be some devatā with some other mission. Garga has said:

    tasmān nandātmajo ’yaṁ te nārāyaṇa-samo guṇaiḥ śriyā kīrtyānubhāvena gopāyasva samāhitaḥ In conclusion, therefore, O Nanda Mahārāja, this child of yours is as good as Nārāyaṇa by his qualities, opulence, fame and influence. You should protect this child very carefully. SB 10.8.19 The two have come to Vraja to help the devatās by killing Pūtana. They did not come to give us happiness, for by giving us up they have created great suffering. The previous happiness is just pain because of the extreme suffering.

    BG 15.9 BG 17.20 BG 18.64 BG 2.62 BG 3.11 BG 12.3 SB 4.29.2 BG 9.11 BG 8.2 BG 17.4 BG 7.8 BG 10.3 BG 13.1 BG 5.18 BG 6.1
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    A cowherd father, asked to account for his son's superhuman feats, reaches for the most reverent category his religious vocabulary allows: 'He must be a deva.' Vraja's love is so absolute that it cannot help under-naming its own beloved — the Supreme is misidentified downward, as a high demigod. Gauḍīya theologians treasure this misidentification as the very signature of vātsalya.

    Stories
    Garga's secret naming

    When Garga Muni came to Vraja to perform Kṛṣṇa's name-giving ceremony in SB 10.8, he warned Nanda that this child was an aṁśa of Nārāyaṇa but instructed him to keep the secret — lest demons find out, and lest Vraja's love be disturbed by knowledge.

    Nanda's verse 23 is the result. He remembers Garga's words just enough to think 'demigod' and not 'Bhagavān.' Gauḍīya tradition: Garga's secrecy is what makes vātsalya-rasa possible. Tattva fully revealed would dissolve the bhāva.

    Important Words
    • kaṁsam — Kaṁsa
      Accusative of Kaṁsa. The verse uses the personal name — without epithet, without title — because the demon has now been reduced to a corpse on the wrestling-arena floor. Gauḍīya tīkā: Kaṁsa's name without title is itself the announcement of his end.
    • nāga - ayuta - prāṇam — whose vital strength was that of ten thousand elephants
      Compound: nāga (elephant) + ayuta (ten thousand) + prāṇa (vital force). The Bhāgavatam quantifies Kaṁsa's strength to make the killing's ease the more striking. Even ten-thousand-elephant strength is, before Kṛṣṇa, līlayā.
    • mallau — the two wrestlers (Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika)
      Nominative dual of malla. Killed in SB 10.44. Verse cross-references the immediately preceding chapter — Nanda has clearly received reports.
    • gaja - patim — the king of the elephants (Kuvalayāpīḍa)
      Compound: gaja (elephant) + pati (lord). Kuvalayāpīḍa, the elephant Kaṁsa stationed at the gate (SB 10.43). Gauḍīya tradition: the gaja-pati at Kṛṣṇa's gate is destroyed; the gaja-pati Gajendra at his own crisis is saved — the symmetry is part of the canto's theology.
    • līlayā — as a game
      Instrumental of līlā. The signature term of Kṛṣṇa-theology. Whatever requires titanic effort from others, Kṛṣṇa does līlayā. The whole acintya-bhedābheda doctrine of effortless creation is condensed here.
    • mṛga - adhipaḥ — the lion, king of animals
      Compound: mṛga (animal) + adhipa (lord). The Lord-of-beasts image — also the etymology behind Nṛsiṁha (man-lion). Gauḍīyas hear an echo: the Vraja-rakṣaka in His Mathurā register reveals the Nṛsiṁha-pulse always implicit in His protection.
    After all, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma killed Kaṁsa, who was as strong as ten thousand elephants, as well as the wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika and the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa. They killed them all sportingly, as easily as a lion disposes of small animals.
    Purport

    Here Nanda means to say, “Not only did Garga Muni declare that these boys are divine, but just see what They have done! Everyone is talking about it.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After all, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma killed Kaṁsa, who was as strong as ten thousand elephants, as well as the wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika and the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa. They killed them all sportingly, as easily as a lion disposes of small animals.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    They killed (avadhiṣṭām) the wrestlers Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika and the elephant who were as strong as ten thousand elephants just as a lion kills other animals without effort.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The wrestlers and the elephant were as strong as ten thousand elephants. They were killed (avadhiṣṭām). This was done without effort (līlayā eva). This was suitable since he was like a lion in relation to other animals.

    Analogy

    Nanda recounts the Mathurā exploits not as a wonder-tale but as testimony — Kaṁsa, the wrestlers, Kuvalayāpīḍa — and the analogy he reaches for is the natural one: 'a lion among small animals.' Vraja-vātsalya knows its son is a lion, even when it dares not call him Bhagavān.

    Important Words
    • tāla - trayam — as long as three palm trees
      Compound: tāla (palm tree) + trayam (three). The bow of Kaṁsa (SB 10.42), broken before the wrestling. The measure is given in tāla — palm-tree-height — because Vraja measures in trees, not in cubits.
    • ibha - rāṭ — a royal elephant
      Compound: ibha (elephant) + rāṭ (king). The simile pairs with verse 24's mṛga-adhipa: lion-king in 24, elephant-king in 25. Vraja's metaphor-bank is animal, not architectural.
    • babhañja — He broke
      Perfect of √bhañj. Same verb used of the snapping of any twig — the Bhāgavatam keeps the lexicon of effort minimal to dramatize the absence of effort.
    • sapta - aham — for seven days
      Compound: sapta (seven) + ahan (day). The Govardhana-līlā's duration (SB 10.25). Gauḍīya tradition reads sapta-aham as the cosmological seven — the duration of a Brahmā's night, the seven prakṛtis — held up on a child's smallest finger.
    • ekena-hastena — with one hand
      Instrumental of eka (one) + hasta (hand). The single-finger detail of Govardhana — vāmena kara-pallavena (10.25) — is here softened to ekena hastena. The miracle is preserved, the cowherd-tongue's modesty intact.
    • girim — a mountain
      Accusative of giri — Govardhana, but unnamed. Verse 18 already named girim; here it returns. Gauḍīyas mark the repetition: the hill that the canto's earlier chapter celebrates as Hari Himself (10.24.35) is here recited by Nanda as a feat-of-the-son.
    With the ease of a royal elephant breaking a stick, Kṛṣṇa broke a powerful, giant bow three tālas long. He also held a mountain aloft for seven days with just one hand.
    Purport

    According to Ācārya Viśvanātha, a tāla (“palm tree”) is a measurement of about sixty hastas, or ninety feet. Thus the great bow Kṛṣṇa broke was two hundred seventy feet long.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    With the ease of a royal elephant breaking a stick, Kṛṣṇa broke a powerful, giant bow three tālas long. He also held a mountain aloft for seven days with just one hand.
    Commentary

    "He broke a bow measuring three tala trees or 60 x 3 hastas. With one hand, his left hand, he held up the mountain for seven days."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Tāla means a tāla tree which is 60 hastas high. Or, Devakoṣa says that a tāla is nine vitasthis (9 inches x 9). He broke the bow like an elephant breaks a stick of sugar cane. He lifted the mountain with his left hand for seven days.

    Related values & verses
    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Bows snapped like sticks, mountains held seven days on one hand — Nanda recites these and his demigod-theory (verse 23) wavers. Vātsalya cannot reconcile a deva of any rank with the ease of these acts, so the chapter is setting up Uddhava's correction (verses 31-43) without forcing Nanda to receive it yet.

    Important Words
    • pralambaḥ — Pralamba
      The demon killed by Balarāma in SB 10.18 — Nanda credits the deed to the dual Kṛṣṇa-Balarāma, never separating them. Gauḍīyas: sakhya-rasa's grammar keeps the brothers' victories pooled.
    • dhenukaḥ — Dhenuka
      Donkey-demon of the Tālavana (SB 10.15). Killed by Balarāma. The list mixes Kṛṣṇa's and Balarāma's victories without distinguishing — a deliberate gesture of brotherly love.
    • ariṣṭaḥ — Ariṣṭa
      Bull-demon of SB 10.36 — same vṛṣa Nanda named in verse 20. Gauḍīya tīkā: the canto cycles its own demons; the second naming is the reverberation of the first.
    • tṛṇāvartaḥ — Tṛṇāvarta
      Whirlwind-demon of SB 10.7 — the one who tried to carry baby Kṛṣṇa into the sky. Nanda's choice to list this earliest demon last in the verse follows a non-chronological order: the demons are recited as they rise in memory, not in history.
    • baka - ādayaḥ — Baka and others
      Compound: Baka (heron-demon, SB 10.11) + ādi (and others). The ādi covers Agha, Pūtanā, Śakaṭa, Keśī — the verse trusts the reader to fill in. Bhāgavata economy: enumeration not exhaustive but evocative.
    • sura - asura - jitaḥ — those who had conquered both demigods and demons
      Compound: sura (god) + asura (demon) + jit (conqueror). Each of these demons had already defeated higher beings before meeting Kṛṣṇa. The phrase quietly demolishes Nanda's verse-23 hypothesis: a mere demigod could not have done what his son did to those who had already defeated demigods.
    Here in Vṛndāvana, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma easily destroyed demons like Pralamba, Dhenuka, Arista, Tṛṇāvarta and Baka, who had themselves defeated both demigods and other demons.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Here in Vṛndāvana, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma easily destroyed demons like Pralamba, Dhenuka, Arista, Tṛṇāvarta and Baka, who had themselves defeated both demigods and other demons.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    These demons were killed by Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma (yena yena).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Ādi refers to Keśī and other demons. It was said that Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma killed the elephant and Kaṁsa (avadhiṣṭām). Because of their mutual affection they are considered as one person, one helping the other. Three verses describe how he helps the devatās. By lifting Govardhana he broke the pride of Indra. This was also for benefiting the devatās.

    Nanda closes his catalog with the Vraja-demons themselves — Pralamba, Dhenuka, Ariṣṭa, Tṛṇāvarta, Baka. Demons who had defeated devas were dispatched by his son līlayā. The list is recitation; vipralambha needs to keep speaking, because silence is the closest approach to His absence.

    Important Words
    • saṁsmṛtya saṁsmṛtya — intensely and repeatedly remembering
      Reduplication of saṁ-√smṛ. Sanskrit's iterative — 'remembering and remembering.' Gauḍīya bhakti-śāstra cites such reduplications as the textual marker of continuous smaraṇa, the practice that becomes its own perfection.
    • kṛṣṇa - anurakta - dhīḥ — his mind completely attached to Kṛṣṇa
      Compound: Kṛṣṇa + anurakta (deeply attached) + dhī (intellect). The technical phrase for advanced bhāva — anurāga. Nanda has now passed from smaraṇa (an act) into anurakti (a state).
    • ati - utkaṇṭhaḥ — extremely anxious
      Compound: ati (extreme) + utkaṇṭha (longing). Same utkaṇṭha-family as gopīs' autkaṇṭhya in verse 5. Gauḍīya tīkā: vātsalya-utkaṇṭhā and mādhurya-utkaṇṭhā share one lexicon — the chapter is binding the two rasas at the level of vocabulary.
    • tūṣṇīm — silent
      Adverb of silence. The narrative gear-change: Nanda's voice stops. Gauḍīya kāvya treats tūṣṇī-mauna at the height of bhāva as a separate sāttvika-symptom, distinct from speechlessness due to ignorance.
    • prema - prasara — the force / spreading of pure love
      Compound: prema (pure love) + prasara (overflowing, spreading). Gauḍīyas treasure this phrase: prema is not a stable possession but a prasara, a flooding-out. Vraja-prema is always too large for its vessel.
    • vihvalaḥ — overcome
      Same word the gopīs were marked with in verse 5 (vihvalāḥ). The chapter brackets Nanda's silence with the gopīs' bewilderment — two faces of vipralambha sharing one verb.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Thus intensely remembering Kṛṣṇa again and again, Nanda Mahārāja, his mind completely attached to the Lord, felt extreme anxiety and fell silent, overcome by the strength of his love.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Thus intensely remembering Kṛṣṇa again and again, Nanda Mahārāja, his mind completely attached to the Lord, felt extreme anxiety and fell silent, overcome by the strength of his love.
    Commentary

    His mind became attached to Krsna. By remembering the powerful aspect of Krsna, Nanda thought, "Oh, by misfortune, I have been separated from my son, who is the ocean of powerful qualities." His attachment to Krsna was such that, unlike Vasudeva, his relationship with Krsna did not weaken even in appreciating Krnsa’s great powers as the Lord, for his attraction to Krsna could not be restricted by that. With his mind attracted to Krsna in this way, he became helplessly under the sway of paternal affection (prema prasara vihvala). In the presence of the supreme prema of Nanda, who like Agastya, swallowed the whole ocean, what is the significance of the ocean of aisvarya?

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    His mind spontaneously became attracted to Kṛṣṇa. Again and again (sam) Nanda remembered the sweetness and how Kṛṣṇa, full of power, protected him. Then the force of prema manifested as tears and choked throat and thus he became silent. He could not speak. Saṁsmṛtya is repeated to show that he could not stop remembering Kṛṣṇa.

    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    After the long recitation, Nanda's words fail. The dam built by speech cracks, and prema floods through — he can only sit silent, body shaking, mind fixed on a son he has just spent twelve verses naming. The Bhāgavatam stages the most eloquent silence in Vraja-vātsalya literature.

    Stories
    Bhīṣma falling silent before Kṛṣṇa

    On the arrow-bed at Kurukṣetra, after Bhīṣma had spoken his long instructions to Yudhiṣṭhira, his last act was to gaze at Kṛṣṇa and fall silent, eyes streaming (SB 1.9.42-44). Speech ended; bhāva took over.

    Gauḍīyas pair Bhīṣma's tūṣṇīṁ with Nanda's tūṣṇīm here. Two different rasas — śānta-tinged and vātsalya — share one grammar: when prema reaches its limit, the verb of silence finishes the sentence speech began.

    Important Words
    • yaśodā — mother Yaśodā
      The personification of vātsalya-rasa. Gauḍīyas understand her name (yaśa-dā, giver of glory) as fulfilled precisely in moments like this — her tears confer glory on her son, not the other way around. Vraja-glory flows upward from the lover to the loved.
    • varṇyamānāni — being described
      Passive present participle of √varṇ (to describe). Uddhava is presumably retelling — though the verse does not record his speech, the participle does the work of indicating it. Nanda recites, Uddhava replies; Yaśodā listens, body weeping.
    • caritāni — the activities
      Accusative plural of carita — deeds, the standard līlā-word. Verse-21 had kriyās (worldly action that slackens); verse-28 has caritāni (Kṛṣṇa's action that elicits tears and milk). The same root family, opposite trajectory.
    • aśrūṇi — tears
      Nominative plural of aśru. The first of the eight sāttvika-bhāvas Rūpa Gosvāmī catalogues. Yaśodā exhibits it as natural response; later sādhakas seek it as a sign of attainment.
    • avāsrākṣīt — she poured down
      Aorist of ava-√sṛj (to release, let flow). Active voice — Yaśodā is the agent of her own weeping; tears are not passively cried but released. Gauḍīya grammar: even bhāva is performed by the bhakta, not visited upon her.
    • sneha - snuta - payodharā — her breasts wet with milk out of love
      Compound: sneha (affection) + snuta (flowing) + payodhara (milk-vessel, breast). The signature phrase of Vraja-vātsalya; identical to SB 10.9.5. The Bhāgavatam declares by quotation that the love is the same love, on either side of the going-away.
    As mother Yaśodā heard the descriptions of her son’s activities, she poured out her tears, and milk flowed from her breasts out of love.
    Purport

    From the very day that Kṛṣṇa had left for Mathurā, mother Yaśodā, though counseled and consoled by hundreds of men and women, could see nothing but the face of her son. She kept her eyes closed to everyone else and cried constantly. Thus she could not recognize Uddhava, treat him with parental affection, ask him any questions or give him any message for her son. She was simply overwhelmed with love for Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    As mother Yaśodā heard the descriptions of her son's activities, she poured out her tears, and milk flowed from her breasts out of love.
    Commentary

    Being able to control himself with gravity, Nanda was able to respect Uddhava as guest in the proper way, to look at him directly, to introduce himself, to ask pertinent questions and to speak about Krsna’s godly qualities. But Yasoda, drowning in the whirlpools of the ocean of unsteadiness, was not able to offer any hospitality. This is expressed in this verse. Continuously tears fell from her eyes and milk dripped from her breasts. In spite of hundreds of men and women giving advice to her from the day that Krsna left for Mathura, she would just say, "I do not want to see anything except the face of my son." Tears poured from her closed eyes, soaking her clothing. She could not ask questions to Uddhava to understand who he was or to make him an object of affection, and could not give him messages for her son. Her breasts (payodhara) flowed with milk out of affection for her son. Payodhara also means cloud. Yasoda was like a cloud showering rain (of tears or milk).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though Yaśodā heard Nanda say that Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma were the best of devatās, she was fixed in thinking of them as her sons. Thus the verse says putrasya caritāṇi (her son’s activities showing power). The word ca indicates she heard about his beauty and sweetness as well. The present participle varṇyamānāni (being narrated) indicates that Nanda started and continued telling the stories without break. She discharged tears abundantly (ava), dampening her clothing since she could not speak, inquire or do anything. This description was also applicable to Nanda and others. Her breasts flowed with milk for a long time, indicating her naturally intense affection.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Hearing that her son was a devatā, Yaśodā could not stop seeing Kṛṣṇa as her son. Rather her affection increased. This shows her intense vātsalya. The present tense is used to indicate that just when the description of Kṛṣṇa began, at that moment she heard. The word ca indicates descriptions of his form and qualities as well. Her breasts began to flow with milk. This shows her intense affection. This continued for a long time. Tears flowed out everywhere (ava), dampening her cloth. She could not question, speak, or do anything. Thus she was different from Nanda.

    Related values & verses
    Related values
    Anahankarah (Freedom from False Ego)Kshama (Forgiveness / Patience)Udyama (Industriousness / Effort)Asteya (Non-stealing / Honesty)Aparigraha (Non-possessiveness)
    Related verses
    BG 15.9 BG 17.20 BG 18.64 BG 2.62 BG 3.11 BG 12.3 SB 4.29.2 BG 2.3 BG 9.11 BG 8.2 BG 17.4 BG 7.8 BG 10.3 BG 13.1
    Personal Guidance
    Analogy

    Yaśodā does not speak. Her body speaks: tears from the eyes, milk from the breast. The same body that fed Kṛṣṇa now leaks the same milk in His absence — vātsalya at its most somatic, the body refusing the lie that the child has gone.

    Stories
    Yaśodā's churning (SB 10.9)

    In the Dāmodara chapter, Yaśodā's breasts overflowed while she churned — sneha-snuta-payodharā — and the milk's overflow was the bodily form of her love for the child at her feet (SB 10.9.5).

    The same phrase returns here in 10.46.28: sneha-snuta-payodharā. The Bhāgavatam quotes itself across thirty-seven chapters: the body that overflowed in His presence overflows the same way in His absence. The substance of vātsalya is constant; the occasion alone has changed.

    Important Words
    • anurāgam — the loving attraction
      Accusative of anurāga. The Gauḍīya technical term for the post-prema stage where love continually finds new sweetness in the same beloved. Uddhava sees anurāga here, in Vraja's vātsalya — and recognizes it as higher than his own Dvārakā-aiśvarya devotion.
    • paramam — supreme
      Adjective qualifying anurāgam. The Bhāgavatam, in its own narration, calls Nanda-Yaśodā's anurāga 'supreme.' Gauḍīya tradition cites this verse as scriptural pramāṇa for the supremacy of vraja-bhāva over all other devotional moods.
    • vīkṣya — clearly seeing
      Gerund of vi-√īkṣ (to see distinctly). Not casual seeing but witnessing-and-recognizing. Uddhava's whole Vraja-mission turns on what he is given to see here; his speech in 30 onward is the report of vīkṣya.
    • nanda - yaśodayoḥ — of Nanda and Yaśodā
      Genitive dual compound. The Bhāgavatam pairs them as a single rasa-unit; Gauḍīya tradition reads this as the model of yugala-vātsalya, parental devotion held jointly. Neither parent loves Kṛṣṇa alone.
    • mudā — with joy
      Instrumental of mud (gladness). Curious word for a man about to console grieving parents — Uddhava's mood is joy because he has just witnessed the highest devotion he has ever seen. Gauḍīyas: the witness of prema is itself a mahā-mahotsava.
    • bhagavati-kṛṣṇe — for the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa
      Locative compound: bhagavati + Kṛṣṇe. The narrator (Śuka) deliberately reminds us that the object of Nanda-Yaśodā's love is bhagavān — even though they themselves think of Him as merely 'son.' The tattva preserved by the narrator while withheld from the lovers: that is the chapter's structural genius.
    Uddhava then joyfully addressed Nanda Mahārāja, having clearly seen the supreme loving attraction he and Yaśodā felt for Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead .
    Purport

    If Uddhava had seen Nanda and Yaśodā actually suffering, he would not have reacted with joy. But in fact all emotions on the spiritual platform are transcendental bliss. The so-called anguish of the pure devotees is another form of loving ecstasy. This was clearly seen by Uddhava, and thus he spoke as follows.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Uddhava then joyfully addressed Nanda Mahārāja, having clearly seen the supreme loving attraction he and Yaśodā felt for Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.
    Commentary

    Observing very closely (viksya) the attraction of Nanda and Yasoda for Krsna, though he was already familiar with high levels of prema, seeing that both in quantity and quality it was superior to that of Vasudeva and Devaki, Uddhava became filled with bliss. He thought, "Now my life has become successful, having seen such love." That is why, though seeing Nanda and Yasoda suffering, he appeared blissful.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    By the way they had acted, Uddhava directly saw (vi—iksya) the prema filled with great thirst (anurāgam) of Nanda and Yaśodā, who were thinking with amazement of the two boys’ condition. He directly saw that they had the highest (paramam) prema for the Supreme Lord (bhagavati), for the form with full manifestation of qualities. Uddhava spoke to Nanda, because he was the chief of the two and Nanda was doing all the talking, whereas Yaśodā could not speak because of great agitation. He spoke to him to console him, in joy. “Ah! This is my good fortune that I have seen such prema.” He spoke in joy, showing only this joyful element, and not showing his distress at seeing their suffering. Since he had a predominance of awareness of Kṛṣṇa’s greatness, he first appreciated the greatness of their anurāga and not that portion which felt intense pain. But the Lord would not have sent Uddhava if he thought he was not capable of pacifying them in their portion manifesting distress.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Seeing such deep prema (anurāgam) of the rulers of Vraja for Kṛṣna, full of all sweetness, his own Lord, whose toe nails are worshipped by Brahmā and Śiva (bhagavati), prema which he had not seen before, he spoke to Nanda in astonishment since Nanda was the main person, or Yaśodā was incapable of hearing, because of her disturbance from affection. Or tayoḥ means they had indescribabl greatness or had the highest prema through a boon from Brahmā when they were Droṇa and Dharā. Nanda was he who gave joy to the universe by his great bhakti or to Kṛṣṇa by his great affection. Yaśodā spread fame by controlling Kṛṣṇa by her affection, tying him with a rope. He was astonished by their high qualication. Ittham anurāgam can also mean “such prema.” He saw the excellent, highest affection increasing again and again, with choked voice and flowing tears described in the previous verses. Experiencing this directly Uddhava spoke with affection (mudā) since he was the best of devotees. He naturally become joyful on seeing the intense prema of the greatest devotees. Or though he should have cried, he showed joy because he was endowed with qulaities of the greatest advisor (uddhavaḥ). He could not otherwise pacify them.

    Important Words
    • ślāghyatamau — the most praiseworthy two
      Superlative dual of ślāghya (worthy of praise). Uddhava uses the superlative, not a polite intermediate adjective. Gauḍīya tradition reads the grammatical extremity as Uddhava's first concession that something here surpasses his own learned bhakti.
    • dehinām — of embodied beings
      Genitive plural of dehin. The praise is set against the field of all dehins — not all devotees, but all embodied beings. The boast is cosmic: no other embodied person carries love like this.
    • mana - da — O respectful one
      Vocative compound: manas (respect) + da (giver). Uddhava addresses Nanda as 'one who gives respect.' A precise observation: even in his grief, Nanda has not withheld honor from his guest. Gauḍīyas: vātsalya does not malfunction even at its limit.
    • nārāyaṇe — for the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa
      Locative of Nārāyaṇa. Uddhava uses the formal aiśvarya-name here — a deliberate move. He wants Nanda to hear that the son he raised is Nārāyaṇa, but he delivers the doctrine wrapped in praise so it does not disturb the bhāva.
    • akhila - gurau — for the spiritual master of all
      Compound: akhila (all) + guru (teacher), locative. Uddhava raises the stakes: Kṛṣṇa is universal guru. The chapter is sliding the tattva in by epithet; the bhāva-protected Nanda receives it as gentle expansion, not contradiction.
    • īdṛśī — like this
      Feminine of īdṛśa — 'of such a kind.' Uddhava points back to the very anurāga he has just witnessed. The deictic refuses abstraction: this love, this specific love, is what is praiseworthy. Vraja-bhakti is always pointed-to, never described in general.
    Śrī Uddhava said: O respectful Nanda, certainly you and mother Yaśodā are the most praiseworthy persons in the entire world, since you have developed such a loving attitude toward Lord Nārāyaṇa, the spiritual master of all living beings.
    Purport

    Understanding Nanda’s mood, as expressed by his statement manye kṛṣṇaṁ ca rāmaṁ ca prāptāv iha surottamau (“I think Kṛṣṇa and Rāma must be two exalted demigods”), Uddhava here referred to Kṛṣṇa as Lord Nārāyaṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śrī Uddhava said: O respectful Nanda, certainly you and mother Yaśodā are the most praiseworthy persons in the entire world, since you have developed such a loving attitude toward Lord Nārāyaṇa, the spiritual master of all living beings.
    Commentary

    "In this world (iha), among the devotees, Devaki and Vasudeva are more praiseworthy, but you two are most praiseworthy because the superiority of your prema." Nanda already said that he knew that Krsna and Balarama were god (verse.23). Knowing that Nanda appreciated Krsna’s lordly aspect, Uddhava describes Krsna in this verse as Narayana, the guru of everyone, thereby emphasizing Krsna’s power, in order to sympathize with their sentiments.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Thus in two verses, Uddhava, first encouraged them by describing Kṛṣṇa’s greatness, taking advantage of similar statements from Nanda. In the universe filled with jīvas (dehinām), up to the great devotees when Kṛṣṇa makes his appearance, Nārada and others are most worthy of praise. Devotees starting with Vasudeva and Devakī and proceeding up to the people of Vraja are even more worthy of praise. Nanda and Yaśodā are most worthy of praise. They are the best devotees (ślāghyatamau). O most worthy of respect (māna-da)! I give respect to you two among all the devotees since you have developed such attraction for Kṛṣṇa. You are glorified by the whole world. Kṛṣṇa is the shelter (āyane) of all the puruṣāvataras including Mahā-viṣṇu (nāra). He is greater than the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha (akhla-gurau). He is the shelter hard to attain, most excellent, most rare, and most auspicious. You are most praiseworthy since (yad) your minds are able to control this shelter of Mahā-viṣṇu who is greater than the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha by your vātsalya-bhāva.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Uddhava speaks for fourteen verses. Some explain as follows. Uddhava stopped up the prema of Nanda and Yaśodā by speaking of the powers of the Lord, defining him in terms of neutrality to the world and seeing him as the soul of all things. This had two goals. He could reduce their suffering by stopping their prema, since their suffering arose from their prema. This would fulfill one of Kṛṣṇa’s orders. That is the first goal. If Kṛṣṇa came to Vraja attracted by their prema, Kṛṣṇa could not fulfil his duties to the Yadus, also great devotees. That is the second goal. But was impossible to stop their deep prema. Great devotees like Uddhava knew this by their experience. Moreover, stopping prema in the devotees will not destroy their suffering, but rather increase their suffering, since prema with its transformations is the form of the highest bliss. The devotee’s joy in prema shines in the Lord. The people of Vraja pray: karmabhir bhrāmyamāṇānāṁ yatra kvāpīśvarecchayā maṅgalācaritair dānai ratir naḥ kṛṣṇa īśvare Wherever we are made to wander about this world by the Supreme Lord’s will, in accordance with the reactions to our fruitive work, may our good works and charity always grant us love for Kṛṣṇa.
